name: Rafael Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or campaigns. Your name stays confidential. Walk me through a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At Oak Lane Accounts I start with builders' bank lines, then match odd items to invoices before anyone signs a return. I like explaining a knotty figure to a client; chasing the same missing invoice three times is the part I grumble about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to lead that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm forty-three, and I did a master's degree and got my chartered accountancy qualification, then stayed long enough to know the building clients by name. I lead three reviewers now, and I still open the original ledger when a number looks too neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners at Oak Lane Accounts that a little faster sorting is useful if someone still signs the tax return. Clients pay us to spot the receipt that doesn't belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm on an ordinary senior accountant's salary, with about three months of bills saved, so I don't expect a small software saving to cost me my post. The mortgage and two school uniforms still make me watch the balance each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing builders' accounts against their invoices and put sixty a month from my wage into the mortgage buffer. If the software saves time, I'd use the spare paid hour to clear the old query list, not promise clients free work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about my job in this picture. The mortgage is a monthly job of its own, but our pay covers it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives you most satisfaction on an ordinary day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A builder came in with a box of wet receipts last Friday, and I made the year make sense to him. I like the moment a client stops dreading the letter from the tax office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the day drag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chasing a missing invoice three times wears me down. I'd be pleased if the routine reminder went out faster, provided I still check what came back.

say: I'd welcome **faster sorting** while keeping a named signer on each return.
I'd use saved time to clear **old queries** for clients.
think: I expect my **senior salary** to hold under a modest tool change.
The **mortgage** still makes me watch our cash.
do: Keep checking **builders' invoices** against each tax return before I sign it.
Save **sixty monthly** from wages for the mortgage and two children's bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about keeping my job.
I still feel **watchful** about the mortgage.
S0.quote: Clients pay us to spot the receipt that doesn't belong.
fieldNote: His pleasure comes from **explaining figures** to clients; routine reminders help only if paid review remains.
Three months of bills give Rafael **room to breathe**, though the mortgage still claims typical senior pay.

steps.text: Keep reviewing builders' accounts against original invoices
Save sixty monthly from salary for mortgage bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Oak Lane to show the team how many returns a reviewer will still sign and what hours the new system saves. A target written only in returns per hour tells us too little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software writes client replies and checks the first pass, a senior can be expected to supervise twice as much for the same pay. I use AI sometimes, but I wait until a method has been checked by someone who understands the tax rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partner for two paid afternoons to learn the new exception screen on closed builders' files, with a reviewer checking my corrections. In the first year of this change, if Oak Lane takes a paid day away, I'd apply for posted senior accounting work at the other firms in town, keeping paid Oak Lane hours until a written offer names a bill-covering wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, not just the junior desk. Three months of savings would disappear quickly if the mortgage kept coming and my week lost a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partner won't pay for those afternoons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the approved tax software and the paper invoices. I won't train on live client data at home or use the buffer to buy a course Oak Lane requires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the junior accountant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to log the corrections the software misses and the time it takes. If management wants a higher target, that record belongs in the meeting.

say: I'd ask for **paid review hours** alongside any output target.
I'd show the partner **missed corrections** before accepting new targets.
think: I could lose a **paid day** even if I keep my title.
Three months of savings would not support a long **mortgage gap**.
do: Learn the **exception screen** on two approved paid afternoons with a reviewer checking corrections.
Apply for **posted town accounting** roles if Oak Lane cuts a paid day.
Keep **paid Oak Lane hours** until an outside offer states wage and start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing paid hours.
S1.quote: A target written only in returns per hour tells us too little.
fieldNote: He will learn after a **paid supervised test** on old files; refusal means using approved tools.
His outside search starts at a **lost paid day** and needs a posted local role with written bill-covering terms.

steps.text: Learn exception screen on closed files during two approved paid afternoons with reviewer checks
Keep approved tax review if firm refuses paid training
Apply to posted local firms if Oak Lane cuts a paid day
Keep paid Oak Lane hours until written bill-covering outside wage and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our clients that full AGI in 2028 reaches the thinking on a tax return before any robot reaches a site in about 2031. A firm still owes them an answer if the numbers are wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Oak Lane to need far fewer accountants, and my senior title won't make tax checking immune. My partner Jo works at the town library, so a lost salary would take most of our mortgage payment with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the garden room instalment and put its hundred a month into cash now. In the first year after 2028, if Oak Lane ends my role, I'd apply for advertised salaried finance-control posts at the regional school trust, keeping any paid Oak Lane closeout work while it's offered until a written offer states a wage covering the mortgage and a start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large part of our household wage to vanish. Three months of bills is a buffer, but it isn't a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a school trust post at less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written wage covers the mortgage and essentials after travel. I won't call an interview an income until there is an actual start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Jo tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Jo that we can wait on the garden room, and I'd show her the hundred going into our cash account. I won't ask the children to solve an adult wage problem.

say: I'd ask for a **named answerer** on clients' returns after AGI.
I'd explain that **tax thinking** changes in 2028, before site robots around 2031.
think: I expect my **senior accounting role** could end in 2028.
Jo's **library wage** cannot replace my whole salary.
do: Save **one hundred monthly** by cancelling the garden room instalment.
Apply for **posted school-trust finance** after layoff only with written pay covering mortgage and essentials after travel, plus confirmed start.
Keep **paid closeout work** while Oak Lane offers it until a confirmed start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing most household pay.
S2.quote: Three months of bills is a buffer, but it isn't a new salary.
fieldNote: He expects his **tax-checking post** to shrink at the 2028 AGI date; physical site robots arrive later.
The cancelled instalment adds **new cash**; school-trust work needs a vacancy, written essential-covering wage and start date.

steps.text: Cancel garden room instalment and save one hundred monthly
Seek posted school-trust work after layoff with written mortgage-and-essentials pay after travel and confirmed start
Keep paid Oak Lane closeout work while offered until new job starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners that five years is enough to decide which client questions still get paid human attention. Full AGI in 2031 reaches our tax reasoning; physical robots around 2034 are a separate problem for builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few years lets me reduce the loan, but I can't bank on a job that might not exist in 2031. I know several firms locally, yet they'll face the same software pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay an extra eighty a month off the mortgage while the two wages hold and ask the school trust whether it advertises paid finance-control work. In the first year after 2031, if Oak Lane cuts my salary, I'd apply only to a posted trust vacancy with a written wage and start date that cover our bills, keeping any paid Oak Lane work while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though less rushed than in the 2028 picture. The mortgage will be smaller only if today's wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification already. I'd take a required school finance module only if the trust funds the fee and paid study time for a posted paid job; I won't buy another certificate on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trust posts no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on any paid Oak Lane reviews and put the extra eighty toward bills if hours drop. I'd ask the partners what work they can still fund, not pretend an unposted job is waiting.

say: I'd ask which **client questions** can still fund review hours.
I'd distinguish **2031 desk work** from physical site work around 2034.
think: Local firms face the **same AGI pressure** on tax work.
Extra warning helps only while our **two wages** continue.
do: Pay **eighty extra monthly** off the mortgage while both wages hold; redirect it to bills if hours fall.
Take a **school module** only for a posted paid role with funded fees and paid study time.
Seek **posted trust work** after salary cuts with written bill-covering pay and start; otherwise retain offered reviews and request funded work.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to prepare.
S3.quote: I can't bank on a job that might not exist in 2031.
fieldNote: Rafael treats the school trust as a **conditional advertised route**, not guaranteed protection from thinking AI.
A required module needs **funded fees** and paid study time; he keeps available Oak Lane pay during any search.

steps.text: Pay eighty extra monthly while wages hold; redirect to bills if hours fall
Take school module only for posted paid role with funded fee and paid study time
Seek posted trust work after cuts only with written bill-covering pay and start
Keep offered Oak Lane reviews and request funded work if trust has no vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is useful if we pay down the mortgage and don't promise the children that a title guarantees work. AGI reaches the accounts desk in 2036; builders' physical work may face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I'd still need a salary, even if the loan is smaller. I'd rather know early whether Oak Lane's paid client reviews can support my lead pay than reach 2036 with a fine job title and no funded hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the extra eighty monthly mortgage payment while both wages hold and ask Oak Lane each tax season what paid review work clients renew. In the first year after 2036, if those fees cannot fund my lead salary, I'd apply for posted salaried finance-control work at the school trust and keep available paid Oak Lane work until a written bill-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a salary I may still need at 53. Ten years of warning helps, but it doesn't make a mortgage disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Jo's library hours fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra payment and use cash for the regular mortgage and food. Paying principal faster is a choice; feeding the children is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Oak Lane now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I like the clients and the wage is steady today, so I'd finish this tax season and check the renewal figures before any move.

I'd keep the **mortgage** in view even with ten years.
think: I may need my **lead salary** at 53.
Client renewal fees could fail to fund my **paid hours**.
do: Pay **eighty extra monthly** while both wages hold; redirect it to mortgage and food if Jo loses hours.
Check **paid client renewals** each tax season.
Apply for **posted school-trust finance** if renewal fees cannot fund lead pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a future salary gap.

fieldNote: His ten-year plan depends on **current wages**; extra principal payments stop if Jo's library hours fall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our tax desk could shrink before I can replace a senior wage. A clear notice period and a real written route into paid school-trust finance would help more than another brochure about skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs for a wrong return after a machine writes it. If the firm keeps my name on the document, it must give me paid time to check the work.

headlineQuote: If the firm keeps my name on the document, it must give me paid time to check the work.
portrait: Rafael is a **chartered senior accountant** who enjoys untangling builders' records at Oak Lane Accounts.
He uses AI **sometimes**, once a tested method and human review are in place.
Typical pay and **three months saved** support his household, but a mortgage and two children keep him watchful.
He learns on **approved paid time** and searches only after hours or fee support fall.
AGI in 2028 brings **expected salary loss**; longer warning lets him reduce debt while wages last.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028** ending his senior tax role before he can replace its wage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **clear notice** and a posted paid finance path with written terms.
